chapter: Theater work, first jobs and recording credits
title: Early failures: mother, father, and his first jobs
summary: He says he could not play at first, his parents' Chicago move, Roy Palmer's funeral job and the New Orleans musicians who encouraged him.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Getting my first drums, with or without lessons

blocks.x: So when you started playing music, you just went into music professionally, you didn't have any other profession.

I thought I was better than I was, I shouldn't have been in the profession. I mean, you see, while I say that, I'm truthful, I couldn't play no trombone, but I just skied and was lucky. I couldn't play.
You never had another job then. Huh? You never had a dead job until later.

Well, at that time I didn't have to work. I had a great mother, you understand. And my mother was a pretty good business woman, and my father was a brick mason, although, he wasn't allowed, they wouldn't give him a card in Chicago, so he started to, he was a foreman at the IC Roundhouse. See, now, doing this blue blood plague around here, all out the Annunciation Street, he laid bricks all out there, you understand, and they had to put in these concrete instead of the top of the floors and the groves and things like that. He made a lot of money here, and we had property almost paid for it. And they decided to, during World War I, you know, the Rampo Street was recruiting laborers, you know, to go up in the stockyards and Swift and all those places. And so we followed the crowd, and we regretted it. I mean, for a while it was really tough, because my mother, I got so she was working and doing her ironing, washing and ironing, you know, and she wasn't used to that. And so, and my father was the foreman. So anyhow, I thought I was good, but I couldn't play. I realized later that I couldn't play. But I was small enough, when I realized I couldn't play, to go ahead and let them teach me, so I could play. See, I couldn't play. I couldn't play. No. When I thought I could play, I couldn't play. I couldn't play. But they just put their arms around me. Joe Olvin, all them guys, put their arms around me. John the Dodd say I never would be a trombone player. See what I'm talking about? But later on, I worked with him at Kelly's table. See, and I left him and went up to Wisconsin Roof, and he tried to get me to come back Chicago and work with him again. I recorded with him. I made him eat up the word. But I don't blame him, because I couldn't play. Now I'm going to tell you a little tale. Roy Palmer got me my first job. We had, as I said, Lionel Hampton carried his drum all the time up on his arms. And Bernie Young, and about four or five others. A woman's husband died, he was a Mason. So Roy said, he was a replacement every Sunday at my house. Charlie Allen, too, was on trumpet. And so Roy said, well fellas, I got a job for you. So we was glad. We was going to get a chance to play in the street. He had been rehearsing for about a year and a half. And so instead of this woman go to the union, get a union band, some fellas could play, she got Roy and Roy got us. So we met right by the union. We were scared, see. And we lined up. So they had augmented the band. Another trombone player, this guy had his mouthpiece over here and a cigarette in here. I looked at this guy and said, dear

We had a mouthpiece over here and a cigarette in here. I looked at this guy and said, I wanted to get this guy to play with this cigarette in his mouth on one side and play on the side. And so we had a little march. So finally Grand Marshal came back saying, fellas, when I whistle, I mean for the drum to start plop, plop, plop, plop, plop, plop, plop, and finally in the bass room, jing, with the cymbals, see. And so this little tune, it went like this. I never will forget this. Ta-da-da-da-da-da-da. Ta-da-da-da-da-da-da-da. Da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da. Da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da. And we just, by the time we got about three or four bars, now this guy with his cigarette and mouth, he had it on the side right next to me, and he was gassing me. I told my cousins, I says, our band gonna play Sunday. So the Grand Marshal came back there, no, don't play no more, fellas, please. So I stayed at the band until I spied my cousins, leaning out the windows, waiting for me to come. I cut out. I cut out. So the next job Roy gave me was playing with Tick Chambers, Richard Jones, and myself, a fella named John Bell, and I think it was this boudreaux and clarinet. Oh, my mother was so proud, and she told all the neighbors, I couldn't play, I couldn't play, I couldn't play. The fellas, the New Orleans fellas just put their arms around me and held me until I couldn't play. So my mother's standing at the big wide green, you know, my boy. I saw, I look at my, I'm frightened to death, I'm trembling. And I said, now kid, don't be afraid. I said, everything's going to be all right. So they started off playing. They said, I played all right, but I don't see how they did it. This was helping me, you know, making me feel good. I played some of the worst trombone I ever played in my life. I was sick that night. I couldn't say, I know I wasn't playing. When you ain't not playing, you know when you're playing right, and when you're not playing right, I couldn't play. When they called me a ham, I was a ham. See? It helped me about them calling me a ham. See? It helped me. It made me practice. Because I might have thought that I was good enough. A fella's never good enough on the menstruants. I know a man in Chicago right now, 82 years old, he practiced six or seven hours a day on the fiddle. And he's been playing for years. See? It's like medicine. A doctor's always something new coming in drugs. And the music has changed, as you know. That rock and roll stuff, you see? Now I don't particularly care for that. But some of them sound kind of decent. Now we had to play, we played uptight, a rock and roll tune. Sometimes we have to play. It's only two chords in it. All we do is sing, uptight, and it's all right, uptight, and it's just two chords in it. See? And everybody looks like they have a guitar now, you know? And they can't do it. It's one of them overnight thing with the guitar. No train or anything like that. Just bling, bling, bling, bling, bling. See now we played for some school kids up in Southern Paul, Illinois. It was some kind of graduation. So we started to play in the Dixieland so the young kids just stood on the side and looked at us. And the middle of it, people danced. So when the fellow came, one of the officials, he said, what can you do with the remedy? They said, all the youngs, they're just looking at you, it seemed like you sound all right, but they let beat. So what we did, we played panamo and all that stuff and rock and roll. See? You know how the drums, the rock and roll, the beat? And then they danced. Then they came out and danced.
